claims.text: A defect- and oxygen-aware first-principles/machine-learning model will predict bulk HfNbTaTiZr conductivity about 10–20% more accurately than conventional perfect-crystal analytical models in both specified temperature regimes.
The starting material is bulk HfNbTaTiZr produced by standard synthesis routes.
The comparison will include a minimally contaminated specimen and a specimen intentionally doped with approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The proposed predictive approach fuses ab-initio and data-driven methods and explicitly represents defect scattering and oxygen-impurity effects.
Quantum and defect-scattering effects dominate conductivity behavior from approximately 0 to 200 K.
Thermal activation and oxygen-induced microstructural changes become significant from 300 to 1200 K.
Oxygen in HfNbTaTiZr produces oxygen-related defects and mild lattice distortions.
Oxygen-related defects and lattice distortions alter charge-carrier scattering mechanisms.
Realistic defect and oxygen configurations cause enhanced electron or phonon scattering relative to a perfect crystal.
Enhanced scattering modifies conductivity relative to perfect, defect-free HfNbTaTiZr.
Defect scattering will lower conductivity in the 0–200 K regime.
Oxygen-induced microstructural effects will modify conductivity behavior in the 300–1200 K regime.
Conventional perfect-crystal analytical predictions deviate significantly from experimental conductivity measurements.
Even a small oxygen concentration increases the discrepancy between conventional analytical predictions and measured conductivity.
The proposed model's stated applicability is limited to 0–200 K and 300–1200 K and to specimens near 1 wt.% oxygen.
Predictions above 1200 K or at substantially different oxygen concentrations remain unvalidated.
The magnitude of accuracy improvement depends on defect-model fidelity and the modeled oxygen-site distribution.
Prior literature on related refractory complex concentrated alloys and refractory high-entropy alloys recommends studying oxygen contamination of their solid solutions.
Prior literature states generically that predicted alloy properties can be tested experimentally.

The hypothesis is falsified if the model is not approximately 10–20% closer to four-probe conductivity measurements than the conventional model in both temperature regimes, or if the proposed oxygen-defect role is not confirmed.
